title: Assessment of chronic bronchitis and risk factors in young adults: results from BAMSE.
ehr_evidence: Questionnaire data and clinical measures from the 24-year follow-up of the Swedish BAMSE (Child (Barn), Allergy, Milieu, Stockholm, Epidemiological) cohort were used; the data source was a population-based birth cohort, not an EHR.
summary: In a Swedish population-based birth cohort (BAMSE) followed to ~22 years of age, early-life environmental exposures (traffic-related air pollution, breastfeeding) and smoking were assessed as risk factors for chronic bronchitis defined by morning cough and mucus production.
key_findings: Overall prevalence of chronic bronchitis was 5.5% (95% CI 4.6–6.3%, n=158) at the 24-year follow-up with no sex difference.
Daily smoking was strongly associated with CB (aOR 3.85, 95% CI 2.32–6.39, p<0.001).
Early-life air pollution (black carbon at age 1–4 years) was an independent risk factor (aOR 1.71 per 1 μg·m−3 increase, 95% CI 1.14–2.57, p=0.009).
Exclusive breastfeeding for ≥4 months was protective (aOR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44–0.99, p=0.044).
Childhood asthma at age 1–16 years was a strong risk factor for CB (OR 3.08, 95% CI 2.17–4.35).
49% of CB cases experienced >3 respiratory infections in the past year versus 18% of non-CB subjects (p<0.001).
No significant association was observed between FeNO levels and CB.
captured_features: Morning cough and mucus production (chronic bronchitis symptoms)
Spirometry FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC and z-scores
IgE sensitisation to airborne and food allergens
Modeled air pollution exposure (black carbon, NOx) by residential/daycare/school address
Smoking status and electronic cigarette use
data_source_type: birth cohort (BAMSE) with questionnaire and clinical measures
population: Young adults (~22 years) from the Swedish BAMSE population-based birth cohort in Stockholm, Sweden
exposure_domain: Early-life air pollution (traffic-related black carbon and NOx), smoking, and breastfeeding
limitations: Chronic bronchitis definition based on questionnaire without a specified time period, differing from the classic two-consecutive-years definition.
Analyses were exploratory and not corrected for multiple testing.
Potential misclassification of asthma as chronic bronchitis.
Self-reported respiratory health events without laboratory confirmation of virus/bacteria.
Critically ill newborns excluded, limiting assessment of extreme prematurity and very low birthweight.
